stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office due to excessive facial hair growth that has worsened over the past several years.  The patient has become self-conscious in public and is very concerned.  She has tried several cosmetic measures, including laser removal and waxing, but the results have been unsatisfactory.  Medical history is insignificant, and she takes no medications.  The patient's last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago, but she regularly has long cycles and otherwise feels well.  She is sexually active with her boyfriend and uses condoms for contraception.  Examination shows moderate obesity with mild hirsutism on the face and chest.  Urine pregnancy test is negative.  The patient is prescribed combined estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pills.  Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which this agent reduces hirsutism?​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​
explanation:
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome

Clinical features

  • Androgen excess: hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia
  • Ovarian dysfunction: menstrual irregularity, polycystic ovaries
  • Insulin resistance: acanthosis nigricans, glucose intolerance/diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome
  • Obesity

Treatment

  • Weight loss
  • Combination hormonal contraceptives
  • Metformin (if hyperglycemia/diabetes mellitus)

Excessive male-pattern hair growth in a woman is called hirsutism.  Hirsutism can be due to increased androgen production (eg, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, Cushing syndrome, ovarian and adrenal tumors), increased local conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), or higher sensitivity of hair follicles to DHT (eg, idiopathic hirsutism).  With excessive androgen exposure, soft, nonpigmented vellus hair changes to coarse pigmented terminal hair in androgen-dependent areas of the body (eg, face, chest, back).

The most common cause of hirsutism is polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), which is often associated with elevated androgen levels.  Combined estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are usually the first choice for treating hirsutism in PMOS.

OCPs work by negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis (ie, suppress endogenous GnRH, LH, and FSH release).  Because LH is what stimulates ovarian theca cells to produce ovarian androgens, OCP suppression of pituitary LH secretion leads to decreased ovarian androgen production.  In addition, the estrogen component of OCPs stimulates the liver to produce higher levels of sex hormone–binding globulin, which binds free testosterone and decreases serum testosterone levels.

(Choice A)  Ornithine decarboxylase is involved in DNA stabilization and repair.  Blockade of ornithine decarboxylase leads to decreased cell growth and increased apoptosis.  Eflornithine is a topical ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor used to decrease the rate of facial hair growth.

(Choice C)  Patients with PMOS who develop diabetes mellitus are usually treated with metformin, which increases insulin sensitivity but does not improve hirsutism because ovarian androgen production remains high.

(Choice D)  5-alpha reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride) decrease peripheral conversion of testosterone to DHT, which can be used to treat hirsutism.  OCPs do not inhibit 5-alpha reductase.

(Choice E)  Testosterone receptor antagonists (eg, spironolactone) are effective in suppressing androgen-dependent hair growth.  Some OCPs contain the progestin drospirenone, which binds both progesterone receptors (high affinity) and androgen receptors (low affinity), thereby acting as a weak androgen receptor antagonist.  However, the primary mechanism by which OCPs reduce hirsutism is negative feedback on the HPO axis.

Educational objective:Male-pattern hair growth in a woman is called hirsutism; the most common cause is polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome.  Combined oral contraceptive pills can treat hirsutism by suppressing pituitary LH secretion and subsequently decreasing ovarian androgen production.​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​
